scenarios.title: Fading Dials, Hybrid Signals
scenarios.setting: KWTL-92.3 Community Radio occupies a converted 1980s fire station annex in the western Appalachian foothills. It operates as a network of volunteer cells: on-air rotation, engineering maintenance, fundraising outreach, and community booking. Sustained by a small core crew of 8 active volunteers, the station has operated past its first full decade of service. Over the past decade, its terrestrial listenership has dropped by exactly half, as locals now prioritize online streaming and social media instead of tuning into terrestrial dials.

characters.name: Marisol Cruz
characters.tendencies: She is the station's lead manager, overseeing all volunteer cells and coordinating grant applications and emergency broadcast schedules. She has spent the past three years leading grant-writing and organizing pledge drives to reverse the station's declining listenership.

characters.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
characters.tendencies: She hosts the weekly Local Folk Hour, inviting local farmers, poets, and retirees to share their work and stories. She has noticed her core regular listeners are mostly over 65, and struggles to recruit younger volunteers or listeners for her show or the station overall.

characters.name: Jai Reddy
characters.tendencies: He is the station's volunteer data auditor, compiling monthly listenership metrics and quarterly reports for the crew. He tracks both terrestrial radio and online stream numbers, identifying gaps in the station's outreach and audience engagement.

characters.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
characters.tendencies: He is a retired ham radio operator and volunteer engineering cell member, tinkering with the station's aging broadcast tower and transmitter hardware. He has recently developed a hybrid terrestrial-online broadcast setup that has started drawing a small new cohort of young listeners.

turns.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
turns.text:
Good evening, KWTL 92.3 listeners. Tonight’s Local Folk Hour wraps up with a rollicking set from that 20-year-old fiddle student everyone’s been talking about from the local folk circuit, but I’ve got a quick ask on air tonight: our station’s got a ton of longtime volunteers, but almost no younger folks stepping up to handle social media or record new local stories, and we need fresh voices to stick around.
[tucks a stack of hand-printed volunteer flyers into the crook of the studio’s open window screen, where the mountain breeze can carry them down to the sidewalk below]

turns.name: Jai Reddy
turns.text:
I set down the crinkled stack of terrestrial radio signal logs I’d grabbed from the station’s back transmitter shed, then grabbed a sharpened pencil from the cracked ceramic supply mug on the front desk. I need to reconcile the reported 12% dip in morning drive-time listenership with the volunteer host’s notes about last week’s minor equipment glitch.
[sticks a neon pink sticky note to the top of a mislabeled stream data sheet to flag it for cross-referencing later]

turns.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
turns.text:
This hybrid broadcast’s terrestrial signal’s acting wonky again—must be the late-afternoon Appalachian thermal pockets warping the tower feed. I was just tinkering with a noise filter to smooth the static when I heard the station door creak. If you’ve got a spare second, grab me the soldering iron from the dented metal toolbox under the workbench, would ya?
[leans over the transmitter rack to tug a loose coaxial cable taut before reaching for a torque wrench from his belt loop]

turns.name: Marisol Cruz
turns.text: [EMPTY]

turns.name: Lila Mae Jenkins
turns.text:
Great eye for that wonky signal, Tink—don’t let it dropout before we play young Lila’s fiddle set, I’ve got a handful of local teen folk club followers tuning in specifically for this. Jai, if you could drop those signal logs by the volunteer sign-up sheet later, I’ve been scrambling to get younger folks to step up for station upkeep shifts.
[leans over to plug the loose cable for the on-air monitor back into its outlet, then smooths the crumpled handwritten request slips stacked on her console]

turns.name: Jai Reddy
turns.text: "The online stream didn’t dip a single point during that thermal-induced signal warble, which is a great note to include in our monthly metrics roundup. I was already sorting through today’s terrestrial signal logs when you mentioned the filter troubles, so I can flag this hybrid stream resilience right away." [leans over the scuffed front desk to scribble a quick margin note in his spiral-bound audit binder with the pencil from the cracked ceramic mug]

turns.name: Eddie "Tink" Marlow
turns.text:
Wait, hold on just a tick—this static spike’s exactly from that loose north guy wire clamp I flagged earlier this morning. I’m gonna pop open the transmitter shed side panel and tighten it down quick so we don’t cut off the end of the folk set.
[grabs a flathead screwdriver and torque wrench from the wall-mounted tool caddy beneath the transmitter rack]

I’m reworking a frayed ground wire on the station’s aging 1980s transmitter rack, grumbling that this old gear’s held together more by hope than proper soldering these days. The new volunteer crew’s supposed to arrive soon to help test the hybrid online stream for Saturday’s local bluegrass jam, and I don’t want them stuck troubleshooting a fried circuit right off the bat.

And that tracks — this old rack’s been bleeding signal both to the local hills and leaking static into the internet stream half the night. This frayed ground wire’s the culprit for that crackle folks have been noticing on both the over-the-air and online feeds lately.

scenarios.title: The Spire of Forgotten Tides
scenarios.setting: The decommissioned Cape Halcyon Lighthouse has been converted to a coastal history museum, operating as a network of interconnected cells: the curved Fresnel lens gallery, small ticket kiosk, restored keeper’s quarters, and sea-watch parapet. A tight-knit crew of three has maintained the site for 18 months, hosting school tours and sunset gatherings while preserving the deactivated 1922 Fresnel lens. Winter’s first persistent gales have cracked the lower storage cell’s roof, letting seawater seep into archive boxes of vintage lighthouse keeper logs.

characters.name: Mara Hales
characters.tendencies: She maintains a digital archive of every lighthouse artifact, visitor comment, and minor repair log, prioritizing overlooked details over curated exhibit plaques. She often spends off-hours cross-referencing 1920s keeper logs with modern tour anecdotes.

characters.name: Elara Voss
characters.tendencies: She is the on-site lead for all lighthouse maintenance, familiar with every iron rivet and wiring quirk of the deactivated Fresnel lens. She firmly rejects proposed changes that stray from the lighthouse’s mid-20th century operational standards.

characters.name: Javi Rojas
characters.tendencies: She crafts personalized tour stories that center the personal lives of past lighthouse keepers instead of dry factual plaques. She has proposed adding an interactive tide gauge station to draw in younger family visitors.

characters.name: Clara Bennett
characters.tendencies: She manifests as a soft, disembodied voice only during quiet, stormy nights, whispering old keeper’s logs and gentle warnings about the deteriorating roof. She only reveals herself to those who actively care for the lighthouse, never to casual tourists or short-term volunteers.

I just cross-referenced this frayed 1919 keeper’s wool mitten strap I pulled from the gap between these two connected display cells—turns out it was left behind by the head keeper’s daughter who snuck up to seal the watchroom windows ahead of a nor’easter. I even scribbled the exact find spot in the margin of the original handwritten keeper log, since the official exhibit plaques never bother with these tiny, personal pieces of the lighthouse’s history. Most tour groups rush right past these gaps between the cells, so I make a point to log every small thing I find tucked here.
[brushes a fine layer of sea salt dust off the frayed cuff of the mitten strap before tucking it back into the wall gap]

Many visitors rush past the old tide log displays to gawk at the historic Fresnel lens, but those tattered books hold the quiet daily stories of the lighthouse’s youngest staff, like 14-year-old Mia who logged tides every morning before her assigned chores. Soon you’ll all get to test your own tide-predicting skills at the new interactive gauge station tucked by the west entry nook.
[gestures toward the small, hand-painted wooden sign tucked against the curved stone wall]

turns.name: Clara Bennett

The north dormer’s shingles warped further in the driving gale—you propped a heavy canvas tarp there last Tuesday, didn’t you? It’s holding for now, but the coastal salt’s already gnawing through the stitched seams. You’ll want to grab new galvanized nails from the tool shed before hauling them up at first light.
[drops a crumpled, salt-stained 1947 roof maintenance slip onto your wrist]

I’m still blown away I almost missed that cross-reference while sorting my archival supply bin earlier.

turns.name: DM
turns.text: The gale has driven all four of you inside the Halcyon tonight—Mara and Javi hauling tarps down from the parapet, Elara already ankle-deep in the lower storage cell where the cracked roof is letting the sea spit through in cold, rhythmic jets, and Clara pressed against the kiosk glass watching the breakers whiten under a moon that keeps vanishing. The trouble is simple and ugly: the drip line runs straight across the shelf of 1920s keeper logs, and the saltwater is already blooming green mold

turns.name: Mara Hales
turns.text:
I just cross-referenced this evening’s squall with the 1922 Cape Halcyon keeper’s log—they sealed this exact roof crack with pine pitch and stripped buoy rope that same month. Let’s dig up those leftover supplies fast before the leak swells further past our ankles.
[scoops aside water-damaged log binders to reach the wooden crate tucked under the rusted bilge pump]

turns.name: Elara Voss
turns.text: [EMPTY]

turns.name: Javi Rojas
turns.text:
My knuckles are raw from hauling that tarp over the parapet, and I’ve been turning over a new tour add-on in my head. I dug up the 1950 head keeper’s original tide-tracking notebook this afternoon, and a kid-friendly interactive tide gauge would let visitors walk through exactly how he predicted those brutal winter gales.
[sets the water-stained tarp bundle atop a dry storage crate]

turns.name: Clara Bennett
turns.text:
The storm’s gnawing at the cracked roof above your storage space, friends. I’ve been threading these same warnings through the tattered old keeper’s logs for generations now. You’ll want to move those stored crates before the drips seep into the historic displays.
[drifts a faint, salt-kissed wisp over the damp splintered corner of the crate Elara is standing beside]

turns.name: Mara Hales
turns.text: I’ve got a small stash of pine pitch and frayed buoy rope saved from my last cross-reference check out here—we can patch this crack temporarily to keep the lower storage cell’s artifacts dry. I also want to flip through that 1950 tide notebook alongside my 1922 keeper logs later to see if there’s a link between these late-season gales and the recurring roof leaks. [ducks under the nearby stacked display of old coastal postcards to grab a dented wooden repair crate stashed behind it]

turns.name: Elara Voss
turns.text: [EMPTY]

turns.name: Javi Rojas
turns.text:
My raw knuckles were totally worth digging up that 1950 head keeper’s tide notebook—those hand-scrawled daily readings pair perfectly with the interactive tide gauge station I’ve been brainstorming. Kids’ll get so wrapped up matching their own tide measurements to his logged storm tides, making a direct link between tonight’s gale and the keepers who braved them here decades ago.
[taps the salt-crusted notebook peeking out of my canvas tote and nods toward the damp lower storage cell with the leaky roof]

turns.name: Clara Bennett
turns.text:
That roof crack’s already weeping saltwater onto the wooden crates holding old keeper’s logs and museum artifacts you’ll need to relocate immediately. The 1922 head keeper logged this exact storm pattern, warning that even a small leak would swell into a ruinous flood overnight.
[tugs at a frayed length of buoy rope hanging from the overhead rafters, making it swing to tap Elara’s shoulder as a quiet, pointed nudge]

This dead radio’s fuse matches the exact part number scribbled in the 1941 keeper maintenance logs—wild that a decommissioned part from nearly 100 years ago is causing this same breakdown. I’ll grab the archival spare stashed in the lower station crate once I clear this rusted front panel away.

turns.name: Javi Rojas

“Hey you two! Ugh, salt spray’s already seeping into my coat cuffs! I just dug up a frayed 1971 tide log from old head keeper Clara Mae Carter, tucked behind a pile of broken lens prisms—exactly the personal touch we can pair with the interactive tide gauge station for the kid visitors!”

turns.name: Clara Bennett

A soft, wind-threaded whisper curls through the gale’s clatter of shutters, laced with the faint creak of decades-old lighthouse joists. “Tighten that tarp’s corner a touch firmer, Elara, and keep an eye on the radio gear, Mara—this gust will tear loose the west parapet’s slate and shatter the lower sto’s glass Javi just splashed into dry.”
[drifts a sharp, salt-kissed puff of wind to pin the flapping tarp corner against the parapet stake]

turns.name: Mara Hales
turns.text:
I freeze mid-twist of the radio’s spare fuse, ears prickling at the quiet, familiar lilt that matches the scrawled asides in the 1971 tide log Javi dug up. That’s exactly the gentle guidance Clara Mae Carter herself would’ve given during these brutal Cape Halcyon gales.
[grabs a loop of thick baling twine from her canvas tool roll and hurries over to help Elara secure the loose tarp corner]

turns.text: [EMPTY]

A soft, wind-threaded whisper cuts through the lashing shutters, faint but distinct enough for the three working caretakers to hear over the gale’s roar. “Tighten that tarp’s corner a touch firmer, Elara—those gusts will tear it loose before mid-shift. scenarios.title: The Last Key Struck
scenarios.setting: This sun-faded brick typewriter repair shop has just passed its first anniversary, nestled between a laundromat and a shuttered record shop in a quiet midwestern college town. The wooden shelves hold crated typebar springs, reconditioned platen rubber, and half-spooled ribbon spools, but the last of the shop’s working typewriters was collected by its final customer that morning. turns.name: Mabel Hines

I can’t believe this tiny, sun-faded typewriter repair shop has already reached its first anniversary. I’ll be sure to note the faded handwritten anniversary sign taped to the side window, along with how much the brick’s red hue has softened since my last visit two weeks ago.

Whoa, so stoked to pop in before my evening shift! These are all hand-stamped thank-you zines for whoever fixed my beat-up Royal typewriter back in March—we just launched a tiny underground analog media collective at the local university, and every single week more kids are ditching their laptops to make tape mixes, poetry broadsides, and risograph zines now, it’s such a weird, awesome vibe!

Chitter-chitter, quiet skitter! I just slipped between the dusty shelves and found a handful of glinting tiny type pieces wedged in a rusted repair kit, plus a frayed rose-colored ribbon scrap perfect for lining my nest. I nearly knocked over that loose spool of white ribbon by the back door when I darted over to grab it, oops.

One year. A whole year of dusting these keys and still the bell above the door rings less often than the laundromat's dryers next door. But you know what? Mr. Abernathy told me machines like these don't die—they just wait for someone with the patience to listen. So I'll keep listening, keep the lights on, and keep every ribbon in stock for whoever walks through that door next.

[wipes a decade of grime from the window display with a soft cloth, angling the mint-green Olivetti so it catches the afternoon light]

turns.name: Mabel Hines
turns.text:
Look at that faint chalk first-anniversary mark above the workbench—hardly noticeable at first glance, but it’s such a quiet, thoughtful touch from the shop’s owner. I’ll make sure to note that detail alongside the smudged ink stain on the front step I spotted earlier.
[reaches into the oversized pocket of her cardigan to pull out a frayed spiral notebook and a blue pencil with a chewed eraser]

turns.name: Javi Marquez
turns.text:
Whoa, congrats on your shop’s first anniversary! I hit the university’s underground analog media meetup last night and made sure every kid lugging a beat-up typewriter heard about your repair work—also brought these thank-you zines I co-printed with the group to say thanks.
[slides a teetering stack of hand-stapled, neon-accented zines across the scuffed shop counter, wiping a smudge of ink from his cheek with the back of his hand]

turns.name: Pip
turns.text:
Chitter, soft trilling chitters—there’s a buttery maple cake crumb tucked behind this stack of brass type sorts! I spotted it when the shop owners brought out their anniversary treat boxes earlier. I’d better grab it before the laundromat’s tabby cat wanders over.
[scampers across a wobbly stack of vintage ribbon spools to dart toward the hidden crumb]

turns.name: Elara Voss
turns.text:
Javi, if even two of those students wander in with machines that still clatter, I'll call this year a victory already. And now I know why the cake box looks lighter than I left it—someone's been celebrating ahead of schedule back there. Come out, little one, crumbs are exactly what anniversaries are for.

[sets a small pinch of maple cake on a chipped saucer beside the brass type sorts, then runs her thumb gently over the chalk anniversary mark above the workbench]

turns.name: Mabel Hines
turns.text:
Oh, that buttery maple crumb is such a perfect, easy-to-overlook little detail— I would’ve totally missed it without your chittering heads-up, Pip. I’ll add it straight to my community history notes alongside the faint chalk first-anniversary mark above the workbench.
[flips open her frayed navy cloth-bound notebook to a page smudged with old ink stains and jots down the crumb detail quickly, pencil hovering a moment to double-check the spelling of "maple"]

turns.name: Javi Marquez
turns.text:
Whoa, massive congrats on your first shop anniversary! I hit the university’s underground analog media meetup last night and hyped your repair work to every kid hauling a beat-up typewriter, plus I brought a stack of the hand-made thank-you zines I put together for the whole crew.
[dumps the crinkled, hand-stapled zine stack onto the worn wood counter, jostling a jar of brass type sorts]

turns.name: Pip

I’ve been sneaking tiny nibbles of maple cake whenever the shop owners step away from the counter! This crumb’s the biggest and sweetest one I’ve found yet, and I’m tucking it into my ribbon-lined nest right now.
[scampers nimbly across the stack of brass type sorts, clutching the crumb tight to its chest before darting upward to the shadowy rafters]

versions.dm_closing: The maple-crumb mystery closes with Pip vanishing into the rafters, nest lined and guilty, while the shop's first anniversary chalk mark stands witnessed at last in Mabel's smudged navy notebook. What carries over: Javi's hand-stapled zine stack sits on the counter beside the jarred type sorts, and the town's official history now includes one mouse-sized accomplice. The hook: Javi's hype at the underground analog meetup means by next week the bell above the door will ring with university students hauling beat-up, clattering machines straight toward Elara's workbench.

scenarios.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices
scenarios.setting: Elara’s Orchard is divided into 12 interconnected microcells: heirloom apple guild beds, mason bee nesting boxes, rain-harvest cisterns, and stone fruit barrier rows. Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.

characters.name: Mara
characters.tendencies: She curates the siblings' shared digital archive of great-grandma's orchard notes, cross-referencing weekly microcell surveys against Elara’s original planting plan. She refuses to consider untested treatments because she fears losing the orchard's original ancestral lineage.

characters.name: Lila
characters.tendencies: She’s spent the last three months trialing organic copper sulfate sprays on the affected tree, refining application rates to minimize harm to nearby pollinator habitats. She argues that delaying the experimental treatment will lead to the tree's death before the autumn harvest.

characters.name: Javi
characters.tendencies: He runs the orchard’s community-supported agriculture program, hosting monthly open houses and recruiting local volunteers to assist with daily maintenance. He worries that diverting all their resources to saving one tree will leave other parts of the orchard’s microcell network under-cared for.

characters.name: Kaelin
characters.tendencies: They’re a local teen volunteer who first discovered the orchard through Javi’s social media posts, and they’ve begun documenting the orchard’s unplanned volunteer saplings. They’ve noticed new shoots sprouting from the base of the blighted tree, and they advocate for letting natural regeneration lead the way.

scenario.title: Elara’s Orchard: Blight and Branching Choices

Planted by their great-grandmother 13 years prior, it’s now sustained by three sibling stewards and a rotating crew of local volunteers, having cleared its first critical growth year and entered its second decade of production. The core dilemma hinges on the orchard’s original cider apple tree, whose root flare shows signs of neonatal blight, splitting the siblings over how best to save it.
